We have developed a simple two-component mixing model constrained by Δ33,36S systematics to quantify the relative contributions of the NC and CC reservoirs to the terrestrial S budget based on Δ33,36S data for MORBs, which we assume to be representative of the bulk silicate Earth, BSE, because any isotopic variations generated during magmatic differentiation are expected to follow mass-dependent fractionation (42). The volatile element concentrations of NC and CC materials were likely highly variable and are not well constrained (51, 52), so we first estimate the mass fraction of CC-derived S in the BSE, f CC S , which can be calculated independently of the S concentrations of the NC and CC endmembers [note that f CC S is not to be confused with the mass fraction of CC materials in the BSE, f CC ; see SI Appendix and (14) for details of this calculation]. Defining the NC and CC endmembers by the mean Δ33,36S compositions of NC and CC iron meteorites, we obtain f CC S = 0.24 ± 0.10 (2 SE). This result—which implies that the majority of terrestrial S was delivered by inner solar system (NC) materials—contrasts with those obtained via chalcogen elemental abundance ratios and mass-dependent isotope systematics, which have been taken to imply that outer solar system (CC) materials were the primary source of terrestrial S (11, 53). However, in contrast to the mass-independent isotope anomalies that form the basis of our estimate, elemental abundances and mass-dependent isotope signatures are susceptible to modification during magmatic differentiation (e.g., see discussion in ref. 12). Therefore, we suggest that the estimate presented here based on Δ33,36S is more robust.

The timing of S delivery: The BSE is highly depleted in S relative to chondritic meteorites (54). This could reflect either the accretion of objects that were themselves S-depleted (e.g., ref. 55) and/or the extensive loss of S from the BSE during planetary differentiation (e.g., ref. 56). Distinguishing between these possibilities has proven challenging due to large uncertainties in the extent of S volatilization and loss during planetesimal accretion and differentiation (55); the magnitude of the partitioning of S between metal and silicate at conditions relevant to core segregation (57–59); and whether large-scale segregation of sulfide liquid from the terrestrial magma ocean occurred (i.e., a “Hadean matte”) (56, 60, 61).

However, depending on the assumed source of the depletion, significant differences in the interval over which the S inventory of the BSE was established can also be inferred. For example, if we assume that partitioning of S into metallic and sulfide liquids during core segregation stripped most S from the BSE, then the S in the BSE today must be from objects that were accreted after the core was fully formed [i.e., from a “late veneer” (62)]. Given estimates for the S abundance of the BSE [~200 ppm (63)] and the mass of late veneer [0.7% of the mass of the BSE (62)], this scenario would require that, on average, the late veneer had chondritic S contents (~3 wt%). Alternatively, if we assume that the S-depletion of the BSE is largely inherited from the S-depletion of the materials that the Earth accreted, then the S in the BSE cannot only sample the late veneer because a late veneer of materials with subchondritic S abundances would not provide enough S to account for its abundance in the BSE (63). Here, we explore whether the observations we have presented can be coupled with constraints from nucleosynthetic isotope anomalies of other elements to better constrain not only the sources of terrestrial S but also the timing of their accretion.

We first estimate an upper limit for the fraction of terrestrial accretion sampled by S in the current BSE based on the model of ref. 37. In this model, accretion proceeds via numerous small impacts, during which new material is added to the Earth and partitioned between the protomantle and protocore. As the core and mantle are assumed to re-equilibrate after each impact event, this model implies that the isotopic compositions of siderophile elements in the BSE mostly reflect the compositions of later impactors; in contrast, the isotopic compositions of lithophile elements represent the average of all accreted materials. For a given element, we can quantify the relative contributions of early vs. late materials to the BSE by calculating the fraction of terrestrial accretion during which the last 95% of that element was added to the BSE (x0.95). This value is a function of the element’s bulk Earth metal-silicate partition coefficient (Dmetal-silicate), the metal mass fractions of the impactors and the Earth (f), and the fraction of each impactor’s core that equilibrated with Earth’s mantle (k) before being added to the protocore.

Combining the estimated S abundance of the BSE [~200 ppm (63)] with cosmochemical estimates of the S abundance of the bulk Earth [~6,350 ppm; 0.12 × CI (63)], we estimate a bulk terrestrial DSmetal-silicate ~ 100. Assuming that f = 0.325 and k = 0.2 for all bodies [such as might be reasonable for larger, differentiated bodies (37, 64)], we calculate that x0.95 = 0.25 (i.e., 95% of the S in the BSE today was delivered during the last 25% of terrestrial accretion). Noting that this model was specifically designed for nonvolatile elements and only considers loss to metallic liquids during core segregation (37), we reiterate that this value represents an upper limit for the fraction of accretion recorded by S, which could also have been lost via evaporation or sulfide liquid segregation (55, 56).

The model of ref. 64 predicts the f CC X recorded by volatile elements, X, as a function of their x0.95 based on nucleosynthetic isotope anomalies of Zn, the most volatile element for which a distinction between NC and CC materials has previously been documented (13–15). To reproduce the observed f CC Zn of the BSE [0.375 ± 0.04; 2 SE (14)], this model requires that the later, CC-rich materials that delivered Zn were enriched in Zn by a factor of ~12 relative to the earlier, NC-dominated and volatile-depleted materials. If this later material was enriched in all volatile elements by a common factor (e.g., by a factor of 12), then the f CC X values of siderophile volatile elements (e.g., S) would be expected to be higher than those of lithophile volatile elements (e.g., Zn). This is because the relative contribution of CC materials increased over time (65), and siderophile elements mostly record the later stages of Earth’s accretion (37).

The calculated values of f CC S (0.24 ± 0.10; 2 SE) and f CC Zn [0.375 ± 0.04; 2 SE (14)] imply that the value for S is similar to—or slightly lower than—that for Zn. Consequently, if the later, CC-rich materials accreted by the Earth were uniformly enriched in S and Zn, then the model of ref. 64 would require that S and Zn record similar fractions of terrestrial accretion. In contrast to S, Zn is thought to have been highly lithophile under the conditions relevant to core segregation [i.e., DZnmetal-silicate ~ 0 (63)]. Therefore, S and Zn would sample similar fractions of accretion only in the limit of no equilibration between the metallic cores of the accreted materials and the terrestrial mantle (k ~ 0). It is also possible that the observed f CC S is much lower than that predicted based on Zn because the CC sources of volatile elements were much less enriched in S than in Zn. However, given the similarity in volatility between S and Zn (6), it seems unlikely that the CC materials accreted by the Earth were enriched in Zn by a factor of ~12 but had S contents similar to the earlier, NC-dominated and volatile-depleted materials.

Alternatively, we consider the possibility that the S abundance of the BSE was established by a late veneer of chondritic material following complete scavenging of S into the terrestrial core and/or sulfide matte (e.g., as suggested by refs. 11, 60, and 61). This scenario is supported by the observation that the chalcogens S, Se, and Te are strongly depleted in the BSE, but occur in chondritic relative abundances in mantle peridotites (11, 54). If we assume that the CC materials accreted by the Earth as part of the late veneer possessed CI-like S abundances [~5.35 wt%; (51)], then the Δ33S and S abundance of the BSE imply that NC materials in the late veneer contained, on average, ~2.5 wt% S [similar to that observed in EL and O chondrites; (51)] and comprised ~87% of the total late veneer mass. This result contrasts with that inferred based on the elemental abundances and mass-dependent isotope systematics of the chalcogens, which have been taken to suggest a predominately CC late veneer. However, it agrees with that independently obtained using nucleosynthetic isotope anomalies of Ru, which imply a predominately NC late veneer (66). Therefore, we suggest that a scenario wherein the S abundance and Δ33,36S of the BSE were primarily set by a late veneer of S-rich (i.e., chondritic) material is most consistent with independent constraints from nucleosynthetic isotope anomalies of other elements. However, given the lack of Δ33,36S data for many of the CC iron meteorite groups, we emphasize the need for additional data to better test these hypotheses.

## Conclusions

While we cannot conclusively identify the mechanism(s) responsible for the distinct Δ33S and Δ36S signatures of NC and CC materials (summarized in Fig. 3), these signatures are inconsistent with ordinary physicochemical processing and most likely reflect the heterogeneous distribution of isotopically anomalous S in the protoplanetary disk. Therefore, they provide a framework for tracing the distribution and sources of S in the early solar system. In this context, the position of the silicate Earth in Δ33S-Δ36S composition space (in between our representative NC and CC endmembers; Fig. 4) implies that its S derives from a mixture of inner and outer solar system materials, in approximately 3:1 proportions.

We document a contrast only in the signatures of NC and CC iron meteorites, but the correlations between the Δ33S and nucleosynthetic isotope anomalies of NC achondrites suggest that these differentiated meteorites also record the heterogeneous distribution of isotopically anomalous S within the NC reservoir in the early solar system. Therefore, a natural extension and test of our observations would be measurement of the Δ33S and Δ36S of CC achondrites. Based on currently available data, we suggest that these materials might possess Δ33S < 0 and Δ36S < 0 (similar to the CC irons). We do not observe a statistically significant contrast between the Δ33S and Δ36S of NC and CC chondrites, but we speculate that this could potentially result from an insufficient sampling of these heterogeneous and unhomogenized primitive meteorites rather than an absence of any distinction.

## Materials and Methods

### Estimation of whole-Rock S-Isotope Compositions.

#### Iron meteorites.

Troilite nodules are the predominant S reservoir in iron meteorites, and ~98% to 100% of S that they contain is AVS (20, 31). Therefore, we have taken the composition of AVS from troilite nodules as a reasonable proxy for the S of the whole rock. In cases where multiple troilite nodules from a given meteorite were analyzed, all measurements are reported individually (i.e., not averaged). However, in cases where duplicate extractions of troilite or duplicate fluorination of AgS2 from a single nodule were performed, these measurements were averaged to estimate the value associated with that troilite nodule.

#### Chondritic meteorites.

Estimates of the S-isotope compositions of chondritic meteorites were calculated by mass-balance of S-bearing extracts (acid leachates and residues) as reported in the literature. Component-specific analyses of chondritic meteorites by refs. 20, 67, and 68 are included in SI Appendix database, but these references do not report uncertainties associated with S-isotope analyses. Therefore, they are not included in our calculations. As described in the main text, in situ measurements made by SIMS are also excluded because they are limited to sulfide grains in chondrites and generally less precise than those made by IRMS.

#### Achondrites.

As in iron meteorites, AVS is the dominant S reservoir in most achondrites. Therefore, whole rock S-isotope compositions of most achondrites were estimated based on analyses of AVS. However, for the aubrites—which are known to contain water-soluble sulfides [assumed to be oldhamite, CaS; (22, 24)]—whole-rock estimates were based on mass-balance of the AVS and water-soluble fractions when both were reported.

#### Quantification of Uncertainty in Whole-Rock S-Isotope Compositions.

As the various references in our database differ in their quantification of the uncertainty associated with S-isotope analyses, Dataset S1 includes a tab (“Unc_notes”) that describes the method by which each reference estimated uncertainties. In general, those associated with IRMS measurement of acid leachates and residues are based on the reproducibility of standard reference materials (e.g., IAEA-S1, IAEA-S2, IAEA-S3), while those associated with in situ measurements are based on either the reproducibility of in-house reference materials (e.g., Balmat pyrite, Canyon Diablo troilite, Anderson pyrrhotite) or repeat analyses of a given sulfide grain. For samples wherein the estimated whole-rock S-isotope composition was calculated via mass balance, uncertainties were derived via propagation of those associated with the individual S-bearing components. As such, the uncertainties associated with these samples are generally larger than those wherein the isotopic composition of a single component (e.g., AVS) was taken as a proxy for the whole rock.
